title: What to pack for North Sikkim
meta_description: A season-by-season packing list for Lachung, Lachen, Yumthang and Gurudongmar: layers, footwear, documents, medicines, cash and what you can hire up north.
summary: Pack layers, not one heavy coat: thermals, a fleece, a padded jacket and a windproof shell, plus a woollen cap, gloves, sunglasses and boots with grip. Carry ID and photos for permits, cash, a refillable bottle and your medicines. Snow boots and long coats can be hired in Lachung and Lachen for about ₹100–300 an item.

sections.heading: Why packing matters more up north
paras: A North Sikkim trip covers more climate in three days than most holidays do in a fortnight. You leave Gangtok at 1,650 m in a light jacket, eat lunch by the Teesta near Mangan in warm sun, and sleep in Lachung or Lachen at about 2,700 m where nights fall close to freezing for much of the year. Next morning you may stand at Zero Point, around 4,700 m, or Gurudongmar, about 5,183 m, in wind that drops the felt temperature well below −10 °C.

Lodges are simple. Most have an electric blanket or a heater, but power cuts happen, hot water may come by bucket in the morning only, and there are no shops to speak of beyond a few village stores. What you forget in Gangtok you will mostly do without. Our list below is built from what our travellers wished they had brought.

sections.heading: Clothes: the layer system
paras: Think in layers you can add and remove in the car, because the vehicle is warm and the viewpoints are not. A single heavy coat is less useful than three lighter layers.
list: Base layer: two sets of thermal tops and bottoms. Wool or synthetic, not cotton.
Middle layer: a fleece jacket or thick sweater, plus a warm shirt.
Outer layer: a padded or down jacket with a hood, and a light windproof and waterproof shell over it in spring and the monsoon.
Bottoms: trekking or quick-dry trousers; jeans get cold and stay wet after snow.
Head and hands: a woollen cap that covers the ears, a buff or scarf, and insulated gloves. Waterproof gloves for snow play.
Feet: two or three pairs of woollen socks and one pair of thin liner socks.
Sleepwear: warm and loose; lodge rooms can drop to near 0 °C at night in winter.

sections.heading: Footwear and what you can hire
paras: Bring one pair of comfortable shoes or trekking boots with a good grip, broken in before the trip. Smooth-soled sneakers slip on ice at Yumthang and on the wet steps at Lachung Monastery. Add a pair of slippers or sandals for the lodge.

You do not need to buy snow gear in Gangtok. Shops in Lachung and Lachen hire knee-high snow boots, long padded coats and gloves for ≈ ₹100–300 an item a day, and drivers usually stop there on the evening before Yumthang or Gurudongmar. Try the boots on with your thick socks. If you have large feet, above Indian size 10, bring your own warm boots, because hire stock runs small.

Check the hired coats and boots before you leave the shop: zips that work, soles without cracks and boots that are dry inside. Return them the same evening or the next morning on your way out of the village, and keep the receipt or note the shop name, because drivers often stop at a different shop on the way back. Prices are usually per item per day and are rarely negotiable in peak weeks.

sections.heading: Documents, money and signal
list: Original government photo ID for every traveller, including children aged 5 and above: Aadhaar, passport, voter ID or driving licence.
Two passport-size photos per person, plus digital copies on your phone, for the permit.
Foreign nationals: passport, visa and the approved Sikkim RAP from the e-FRRO portal.
Cash: ATMs are in Gangtok and Mangan, and occasionally in Chungthang, but not reliable up north. Carry enough for snow gear, Zero Point, tips and snacks: about ₹3,000–5,000 per person.
Phone: BSNL and Jio usually work in Lachung and Lachen, but signal fades on the high roads. Download offline maps and tell family you may be out of reach for a day.
A power bank, because charging can be limited during power cuts.

sections.heading: Health kit for altitude
paras: Altitude is the main health risk in North Sikkim. Pack a small kit and talk to your doctor before the trip if you have any heart, lung or blood pressure condition, or if you want to carry medicine for altitude sickness.
list: Your regular medicines, with a few days' spare in case a road closes.
Paracetamol, an anti-nausea tablet, oral rehydration salts and something for an upset stomach.
Motion sickness tablets; the roads are long and winding.
Lip balm with SPF, sunscreen of SPF 30 or more, moisturiser and saline nasal spray for the dry air.
Sunglasses with UV protection, essential on snow.
Any prescription for altitude medicine from your own doctor, not borrowed on the road.

sections.heading: For children, seniors and photographers
paras: Families should pack a few extras. Children lose heat faster than adults, so bring one more layer per child than you think you need, plus spare gloves, because wet gloves after snow play are the most common complaint we hear. Familiar snacks and a small toy or book help on long drive days. Remember that children under 5 are not permitted in North Sikkim at all, and children aged 5 and above need ID.

Seniors will be glad of a small cushion and a neck pillow for the drives, a walking stick with a rubber tip for icy paths, and a hot water bottle filled at the lodge on cold nights. Keep regular medicines in the handbag, not the roof luggage, with a written list of doses and doctors' numbers.

Photographers should carry spare batteries and keep them in an inside pocket, because cold drains them quickly at Zero Point and Gurudongmar. A lens cloth, a rain cover for the camera in spring and the monsoon, and a small tripod for the clear November nights in Lachung are worth the space. Drones need permission and are generally not allowed near the border areas, so leave yours in Gangtok unless you have written clearance.

sections.heading: Small things that make a big difference
paras: A refillable bottle is not optional. The local bodies in Lachung and Lachen have restricted packaged plastic water bottles at times, and you will need 3 to 4 litres a day to stay hydrated at altitude. A small insulated flask for warm water on the Gurudongmar dawn drive is worth its weight.

Pack dry snacks: biscuits, nuts, dried fruit, chocolate. Shops are few and the Gurudongmar and Yumthang mornings start before breakfast. A torch or headlamp helps during power cuts and 4 am departures. Carry a cloth bag to take your rubbish back to Gangtok, because there are few bins up north. Keep a small daypack for the excursion, and leave the big bags in the lodge.

Finally, pack light. North Sikkim vehicles carry luggage on the roof under a tarpaulin, and one soft bag per person of 15 kg or less is easier for the driver and kinder on the narrow stairs of mountain lodges. Leave a bag with your Gangtok hotel if you are returning there.

faqs.q: What clothes should I wear in North Sikkim?
faqs.a: Wear layers: thermal base layers, a fleece or thick sweater, a padded or down jacket with a hood and a windproof shell. Add a woollen cap, a scarf, insulated gloves and woollen socks. Trekking trousers work better than jeans. Even in May and October, mornings at Yumthang and Gurudongmar can be well below freezing.

faqs.q: Can I hire snow boots in Lachung?
faqs.a: Yes. Shops in Lachung and Lachen hire knee-high snow boots, long padded coats and gloves for about ₹100–300 an item a day. Drivers usually stop there the evening before the excursion. Try boots on with thick socks. If your feet are larger than Indian size 10, bring your own warm boots.

faqs.q: How cold is North Sikkim in December?
faqs.a: In December, Lachung and Lachen range from about −5 °C at night to 8 °C by day, often with snow. Yumthang is colder, and Zero Point and Gurudongmar fall to −15 °C or below with strong wind. Pack a down jacket, waterproof gloves, thermals and warm boots, and expect some roads above the villages to close after snow.

faqs.q: Do I need cash in North Sikkim?
faqs.a: Yes. ATMs are reliable in Gangtok and Mangan but not up north, and many small shops and gear-hire stalls take only cash. Carry about ₹3,000–5,000 per person for snow gear, Zero Point, tips and snacks. Some lodges accept UPI when the signal works, but do not count on it.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network in Lachung and Lachen?
faqs.a: BSNL and Jio usually work in Lachung and Lachen villages, and Airtel sometimes. Signal fades on the high roads to Yumthang, Zero Point and Gurudongmar, and during power cuts towers may go down. Download offline maps, keep a power bank, and tell family you may be out of reach for a day.

faqs.q: Should I carry water bottles to North Sikkim?
faqs.a: Carry a refillable bottle rather than packaged ones. The local bodies in Lachung and Lachen have restricted packaged plastic water bottles at times, and you need 3 to 4 litres a day at altitude. Lodges provide drinking water for refills. A small insulated flask is useful for the cold Gurudongmar dawn.

faqs.q: What medicines should I take to North Sikkim?
faqs.a: Take your regular medicines with a few spare days, paracetamol, anti-nausea and motion sickness tablets, oral rehydration salts and something for an upset stomach. Add sunscreen, lip balm and saline nasal spray. If you want altitude medicine, get a prescription from your own doctor before the trip, especially with any health condition.

faqs.q: What shoes are best for Yumthang and Zero Point?
faqs.a: Trekking boots or shoes with a deep, grippy sole, broken in before the trip. Smooth sneakers slip on ice and wet steps. In snow season, hire knee-high snow boots in Lachung for about ₹100–300 a day. Bring slippers or sandals for the lodge and woollen socks for the cold mornings.

faqs.q: How much luggage can I take to North Sikkim?
faqs.a: Pack one soft bag of 15 kg or less per person. North Sikkim SUVs carry luggage on the roof under a tarpaulin, and mountain lodges have narrow stairs. Leave larger suitcases at your Gangtok hotel if you are coming back that way, and keep a small daypack for the excursion mornings.
